html:
From about 1640 to the American Revolution, the merchants of New England lived by carrying goods across the Atlantic, much as the Dutch did in Europe. Their thin, rocky soil could not grow a great export crop, so they turned to the sea.

The trade worked like this:

  • Fishermen caught cod off the Grand Banks; the best went to Spain and Portugal, the worst fed enslaved people in the Caribbean.
  • Ships built cheaply from New England timber carried fish, wood and food to the sugar islands.
  • They brought back molasses, which Boston and Newport distilled into rum, some of it shipped to Africa in the slave trade.

London wanted colonial trade to run through English ports. The Navigation Acts from 1651 and the tax on foreign molasses in 1733 were widely dodged by smuggling. When Britain began enforcing them after 1763, Boston's merchants led the protests. The Boston Tea Party of 1773 helped bring on the war that ended in independence.
